Outcome_variable.evidence_source: [/page/2/Text/2] Subjective well-being encompasses mental states that are positive (e.g., life satisfaction) and negative (e.g., depression). Most empirical studies of subjective wellbeing have focused on self-report assessments (Lucas & Diener, 2004). These studies have been particularly interested in the positive effects discerned from examining children's own assessments on measures such as life satisfaction or happiness (Axford et al., 2014).[/page/2/Text/3] To measure subjective well-being, most scholars have used children's general life satisfaction as an indicator (e.g., Casas & González-Carrasco, 2019; Ferguson, Kasser, & Jahng, 2011; Park & Huebner, 2005) because it is a holistic, useful, and reliable indicator of subjective well-being (Cummins, 2018).
